english_translation: This child reads well and enjoys writing short stories.

dialogue.shona: Mwana uyu anoverenga zvakanaka uye anofarira kunyora nyaya pfupi.
dialogue.english: This child reads well and enjoys writing short stories.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Mwana [child] • uyu [uyu] • anoverenga [he/she verenga] • zvakanaka [well / nicely / very good] • uye [and / furthermore] • anofarira [he/she farira] • kunyora [to / at nyora] • nyaya [nyaya] • pfupi [pfupi]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakanaka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anoverenga')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anoverenga' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Pointing Out Things: Demonstratives ('uyu' = 'this / that / here')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, words for 'this/these' and 'that/those' (like 'uyu') come AFTER the noun they point to and mirror the noun's group! Near demonstratives ('this / these / right here') repeat the noun class vowel: 'mwana uyu' (this child), 'nyama iyi' (this meat), 'kapu iyi' (this cup), 'bhuku iri' (this book), 'zvinhu izvi' (these things). Replacing the final vowel with '-o' shifts the meaning to 'that / those / there': 'uyo' (that person), 'iyo' (that one), 'uko' (over there).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Near Demonstrative ('uyu/iyi/iri/ichi/izvi' = this/these) | replace final vowel with '-o' ('uyo/iyo/iro/icho/izvo' = that/those)

cultural_notes.title: Creative Writing & Short Stories ('Nyaya Pfupi') in Shona Literature
cultural_notes.content: Shona has a vibrant literary tradition of novels and short stories ('nyaya pfupi') pioneered by authors like Solomon Mutswairo, Patrick Chakaipa, and Charles Mungoshi, and schools actively encourage pupils to read and compose their own stories.

active_exercises.explanation: Because 'mbuya' takes the respectful 'va-' agreement, 'our grandmother' is 'mbuya vedu' ('va-' + '-edu').

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new family sentence into English: 'Hanzvadzi yangu inoshanda muguta reHarare.'
options: My parents live at the rural homestead in Masvingo.
My sibling works in the city of Harare.
My friend passed all her school examinations this year.
The baby is sleeping quietly inside the bedroom.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My sibling works in the city of Harare.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Hanzvadzi yangu' = 'My sibling (brother/sister)', 'inoshanda' = 'works', 'muguta reHarare' = 'in the city of Harare'.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).
